items.claim: OS command injection lets an attacker inject arbitrary operating system commands into a shell command built from unvalidated user input, giving full control of the host web server.
items.body: When an application passes user-controllable data into a shell command interpreter (system(), exec(), cmd.exe), an attacker can use shell metacharacters (pipes, semicolons, backticks, &&) to append or alter commands. The chained commands execute with the application's privileges, enabling reading or modifying all data, installing backdoors, and performing privileged actions if the process is over-privileged. Variants include argument injection (input used as an argument to a fixed program, where separators are not stripped) and full command selection. Prevention: never call OS commands from application code; use library APIs; if unavoidable, strict allowlist input validation and proper quoting of arguments. Never rely on escaping/sanitizing shell metacharacters.
items.disproof: If user-supplied input is never passed to a shell, if commands are built from fixed allowlisted values, or if metacharacters are stripped with a validated allowlist of permitted characters, injection is neutralized. A successful request showing only the intended fixed command (and no appended shell output) disproves exploitation.

sources.quote: Operating system command injection vulnerabilities arise when an application incorporates user-controllable data into a command that is processed by a shell command interpreter. If the user data is not strictly validated, an attacker can use shell metacharacters to modify the command that is executed, and inject arbitrary further commands that will be executed by the server.
This weakness can lead to a vulnerability in environments in which the attacker does not have direct access to the operating system, such as in web applications.
The most effective way to prevent OS command injection vulnerabilities is to never call out to OS commands from application-layer code.
